Editor's note: Campbell Brown anchors CNN's "Campbell Brown: No Bias, No Bull" at 8 p.m. ET Mondays through Fridays. She delivered this commentary during the "Cutting through the Bull" segment of Monday night's broadcast. CNN's Campbell Brown says nonemergency legislation needs time to be read by the public and Congress. (CNN) -- Whether by omission or commission, both the White House and Congress get a dose of blame for not living up to the new era of transparency promised by President Obama. The president's old campaign Web site still has this commitment there for all to see: . "As president, Obama will not sign any nonemergency bill without giving the American public an opportunity to review and comment on the White House Web site for five days." Well, the president broke that promise barely a week after taking office when he signed the Lilly Ledbetter Bill dealing with equal pay for men and women. A good bill, and certainly one that could have survived a five-day comment period. So, maybe the White House folks just forgot? But then there is Congress and the Stimulus Bill. How fast could you get through it? According to the nonpartisan Sunlight Foundation, lawmakers had just 13 hours to read 1,100 pages of material that would cost the American taxpayer $787 billion. That's less than a minute and a half per page, with no time for bathroom breaks. No wonder so many of our lawmakers didn't seem to notice that last-minute exemption clearing the way for bailed-out companies like AIG to pay out big bonuses. So, the House tried to clean up the mess last week by rushing through another bill -- a tax on AIG bonuses. That bill was just 11 hours old before it went on the floor to be argued and then quickly approved. And the list goes on well before the president took office. The bank bailout got all of 29 hours, the rescue of Fannie and Freddie was only available for 19 hours. This is how bills could literally become, to borrow a phrase, too big to fail -- and too fast to stop. The Sunlight Foundation is calling on Congress to allow the American people three days, 72 hours, to read a nonemergency bill online before debate begins. We strongly agree. And yes lawmakers, you can have three days to read it over, too, before taking a stand. As for President Obama's promise of a five-day public review once a bill leaves Capitol Hill headed for his desk, it would be nice if he kept his word on this going forward. The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Campbell Brown.

**Editor’s note:** Campbell Brown anchors CNN’s *Campbell Brown: No Bias, No Bull* at 8 p.m. ET, Monday through Friday. She delivered this commentary during the “Cutting Through the Bull” segment of Monday night’s broadcast.

**CNN’s Campbell Brown argues that the public and Congress need sufficient time to review nonemergency legislation.**

(CNN) — Whether through omission or commission, both the White House and Congress deserve blame for failing to live up to the new era of transparency promised by President Obama.

The president’s former campaign website still displays this commitment for all to see:

> “As president, Obama will not sign any nonemergency bill without giving the American public an opportunity to review and comment on the White House Web site for five days.”

Yet the president broke that promise barely a week after taking office, when he signed the Lilly Ledbetter Bill addressing equal pay for men and women. It was a good bill—and certainly one that could have survived a five-day public comment period.

Perhaps White House officials simply forgot?

Then there is Congress and the stimulus bill. How quickly could you read it? According to the nonpartisan Sunlight Foundation, lawmakers had just 13 hours to review 1,100 pages of material that would cost American taxpayers $787 billion. That amounts to less than a minute and a half per page, with no time for bathroom breaks.

No wonder so many lawmakers appeared not to notice the last-minute exemption that cleared the way for bailed-out companies such as AIG to award large bonuses.

The House tried to clean up the mess last week by rushing through yet another bill—a tax on AIG bonuses. That bill was only 11 hours old when it reached the floor for debate and was then quickly approved.

And the pattern began well before the president took office. The bank bailout received just 29 hours of review, while the rescue package for Fannie and Freddie was available for only 19 hours.

This is how bills can literally become, to borrow a phrase, too big to fail—and move too quickly to stop.

The Sunlight Foundation is calling on Congress to give the American people three days—72 hours—to read a nonemergency bill online before debate begins. We strongly agree.

And yes, lawmakers, you may have those three days to read it as well before taking a position.

As for President Obama’s promise to provide a five-day public review period once a bill leaves Capitol Hill and heads to his desk, it would be welcome if he kept his word going forward.

*The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Campbell Brown.*
outputs.L2:
**Editor’s note:** Campbell Brown hosts CNN’s *“Campbell Brown: No Bias, No Bull”* at 8 p.m. ET, Monday through Friday. She presented the following opinion during the “Cutting Through the Bull” portion of Monday evening’s program.

**(CNN) —** Campbell Brown argues that Congress and the public should be given adequate time to examine legislation that does not involve an emergency.

Through either deliberate action or simple neglect, both Congress and the White House deserve criticism for failing to meet the standard of openness President Obama pledged to establish.

His former campaign website still displays this promise: “As president, Obama will not sign any nonemergency bill without giving the American public an opportunity to review and comment on the White House Web site for five days.”

Yet little more than a week after entering office, Obama failed to honor that commitment when he signed the Lilly Ledbetter Bill, which addressed equal pay for women and men. It was worthwhile legislation and surely could have withstood five days of public scrutiny. Perhaps White House officials simply overlooked the pledge.

Congress’s handling of the stimulus package raises an even bigger concern. How quickly could anyone reasonably read it? The nonpartisan Sunlight Foundation reported that legislators were allowed only 13 hours to review 1,100 pages authorizing $787 billion in taxpayer spending. That works out to under 90 seconds per page—even without stopping for a bathroom break.

It is hardly surprising, then, that many members of Congress apparently missed a provision added at the last moment that allowed companies receiving bailout money, including AIG, to award large bonuses.

The House attempted to repair the damage the following week by rapidly advancing another measure that would tax AIG bonuses. That proposal had existed for only 11 hours before reaching the House floor for debate, after which it was swiftly passed.

The same pattern predates Obama’s presidency. Lawmakers had only 29 hours to examine the bank bailout, while the Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac rescue plan was available for just 19 hours.

Using a familiar expression, this is how legislation can become not only “too big to fail,” but also too rushed to prevent.

The Sunlight Foundation has urged Congress to post nonemergency bills online for 72 hours—three full days—so Americans can review them before debate starts. We fully support that proposal. Members of Congress should also use those three days to study the legislation before deciding where they stand.

Obama, meanwhile, promised to provide a five-day period for public review after legislation leaves Capitol Hill and arrives at the White House. From this point forward, it would be good to see him fulfill that commitment.

The views stated in this commentary belong exclusively to Campbell Brown.
outputs.L3:
The White House and Congress failed to uphold President Barack Obama’s promise to bring greater transparency and public scrutiny to the legislative process. During his campaign, Obama pledged that nonemergency legislation would be made publicly available for five days before he signed it, giving citizens time to examine and comment on proposed laws. Yet early in his presidency, he departed from that commitment by quickly signing the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act without allowing the promised five-day review period.

Congress likewise moved major legislation forward with little time for careful examination. Lawmakers reportedly had only 13 hours to review the 1,100-page, $787 billion economic stimulus bill before voting on it. Such haste made it difficult to identify significant provisions, including language that helped preserve contractual bonuses for executives at the insurance giant AIG. After those bonuses provoked public outrage, Congress responded with equal speed, advancing legislation to tax them after allowing only about 11 hours for review and debate.

This pattern was not limited to the stimulus package or the AIG controversy. Other consequential measures, including the bank bailout and the rescue of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, were also made available for only brief periods before legislative action. Taken together, these episodes suggest that, despite promises of openness and deliberation, both the executive and legislative branches repeatedly prioritized speed over meaningful public review and careful scrutiny.
outputs.L4:
Campbell Brown argues that both the White House and Congress have failed to live up to their promises of transparency. During the campaign, President Obama pledged that the public would have an opportunity to review nonemergency legislation before he signed it. Yet several major bills have moved through Washington so quickly that neither citizens nor, in some cases, members of Congress had enough time to understand what they contained.

The pattern began with the Lilly Ledbetter equal-pay legislation and continued with the enormous economic stimulus package. Although the stimulus bill involved hundreds of billions of dollars and ran to more than a thousand pages, lawmakers were given only a short period to examine the final version before voting. Similar urgency surrounded financial-bailout measures and legislation responding to bonuses paid by AIG. Rather than allowing for careful review, political leaders repeatedly argued that immediate action was essential.

Brown does not dispute that a genuine emergency can require the government to act quickly. Her concern is that officials have begun treating nearly every important proposal as an emergency, using haste to avoid scrutiny and debate. When Congress votes on complex legislation before members have read it, lawmakers cannot fully understand the consequences, challenge questionable provisions, or explain their decisions to the public.

The AIG bonus controversy illustrates the danger. A provision protecting certain bonus payments was included in bailout-related legislation and attracted little attention before the bill passed. Only after the bonuses became public did lawmakers express outrage and rush to reverse course. Had the legislation been available for meaningful examination, the exemption might have been noticed, debated, and removed before becoming law.

The problem, Brown concludes, is not merely procedural. Rushed lawmaking can produce expensive mistakes, contradictory policies, and angry attempts to repair problems after the fact. It also weakens accountability: elected officials can hardly be held responsible for legislation they were not given a reasonable chance to read.

Major bills—especially those involving vast sums of public money—should therefore be posted publicly and left open for review before a vote or presidential signature. Transparency promises matter most when the stakes are high. If the White House and Congress want the public to trust their decisions, they must stop using urgency as a routine excuse and give citizens and lawmakers enough time to know what the government is doing.

### Campbell Brown: A Career in Journalism and Media

Campbell Brown is an American journalist, editor, and media executive known for her work in television news and digital publishing. She began her career as a reporter and later became a prominent anchor at NBC News and CNN, covering major political and international events.

After leaving television, Brown focused on education journalism and co-founded *The 74*, a nonprofit news organization covering education policy in the United States. She later joined Facebook—now Meta—where she led news partnerships and worked with editors and publishers to navigate the changing digital media landscape.

Throughout her career, Campbell Brown has played an influential role in the evolution of modern journalism, connecting traditional editorial standards with new online platforms.
